common_name: Dancing in the Moonlight Hosta (Ruffled Blue-Green Hosta with Cream Margin)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Dancing in the Moonlight forms a medium-size mound of intensely ruffled, deeply folded, glaucous blue-green leaves edged in a wide creamy white margin, with twisted leaf tips that catch the light and give the clump a frosted, textured look. Near-white, lightly striped flowers rise on scapes in mid-summer, though the richly textured foliage remains the main attraction all season. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; the wavy margin and blue cast are most pronounced with a few hours of gentle morning sun followed by afternoon shade. Registered by hybridizer Hans Hansen of Walters Gardens, it provides strong textural contrast among smoother-leaved hosta companions.

common_name: Liam's Smile Hosta (Olive-Green Hosta with Wine-Red Petioles)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Liam's Smile forms a medium clump of ruffled, olive-green leaves carried on glossy wine-red petioles, with the red color bleeding upward into the leaf veins and, in cool spring weather, sometimes flushing the margins or even the whole leaf with purple before it settles to green for summer. It is one of the more reliable hosta blushers across a wide range of climates, coloring up even in warmer gardens where many red-petioled hostas fade to plain green. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and give it a few seasons to bulk up into a full, textured mound. Lavender flowers appear on scapes in summer, but the petiole and vein color are the real draw.

common_name: Granny's Goosebumps Hosta (Heavily Corrugated Wide-Spreading Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, allowing generous room for the wide-spreading mound.

directions: Granny's Goosebumps is grown for its intensely corrugated, large, irregularly shaped leaves whose bumpy, puckered surface gives the cultivar its name; new growth emerges chartreuse before settling to green as the leaves mature through the season. The wide, low, spreading mound holds its leaves out nearly horizontally, showing off the heavy texture to best effect, and pale lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, allowing ample room for the clump to spread well beyond its initial planting size. Its strongly textured surface makes it a good foil for smooth- or glossy-leaved hosta companions nearby.

common_name: Lord Puckersheen Hosta (Glossy Dark Green Puckered Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Lord Puckersheen carries broad, shiny, dark green leaves marked by deep veins and heavy ripples that give each leaf a pronounced puckered, light-catching texture. The large, substantial mound builds into an imposing clump over several seasons and sends up pale lavender flowers on tall scapes in summer. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the glossy dark foliage holds its color well and provides a bold textural anchor among finer-textured or variegated hosta neighbors. Bred by Wisconsin hybridizer Charlie Kwick from a cross of 'Sagae' and 'Captain Kirk', it is distributed through several specialty hosta nurseries.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving this giant cultivar ample room to reach full size over several years.

directions: Mint Rushmore is a giant hosta registered by Monty and Julie Carlson, bred from a cross of 'Komodo Dragon' and 'Jade Cascade' crossed again with 'Bright Lights' and 'Lakeside Delight', producing a massive mound of substantial, minty-green leaves. Like other giant hostas it needs several years and generous room to reach its full spread, building slowly into an imposing specimen rather than filling in quickly. Near-white flowers appear on tall scapes above the foliage in summer, though the huge leaf size is the main attraction. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and use it as a dramatic focal point where its mature size can be fully appreciated.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright to full shade; established clumps tolerate dry shade well.

directions: Sandy Claws is a dwarf, spreading selection of the normally clump-forming Epimedium wushanense, producing long, lance-shaped, spiny-margined evergreen leaves that emerge a dramatic chocolate-maroon in spring before mellowing to dark green by summer. Thickly packed panicles of large, creamy yellow, spidery flowers are held just above the foliage in spring. Unlike most epimediums, which clump slowly, this selection spreads steadily to form a substantial patch over several years, making it useful as a textural groundcover in dry shade. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright to full shade; it tolerates drought well once established and holds its spiny evergreen foliage through winter in milder climates.

common_name: Ninja Stars Epimedium (Spiny Evergreen Barrenwort with Yellow Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Ninja Stars is a vigorous Darrell Probst hybrid of two Sichuan-collected epimedium species, forming a dense crown of long, narrow, spiny-edged evergreen leaflets that emerge bronze in spring before turning semi-glossy dark green. Numerous erect stems carry large, bright yellow flowers held well above the foliage in spring, a showier display than many epimediums. The multi-branched rhizomes spread modestly each year, slowly building a weed-suppressing patch in dry shade. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; it is reliably cold hardy and holds its spiny evergreen foliage through winter in most of its range.

common_name: Touch of Pink Astilbe (Compact Pale Pink Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade.

directions: Touch of Pink forms an upright, compact mound of dark green, finely dissected foliage topped by dense, uniform plumes of light pink flowers that open freely and continuously over a long late-summer season. Bred in the Netherlands in 1992 from a cross of Astilbe simplicifolia 'Hennie Graafland' (pollen parent) and Astilbe japonica 'Europa' (seed parent), it was selected specifically for its tidy, free-flowering habit compared with older astilbe hybrids. Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, since astilbe foliage scorches quickly if the soil is allowed to dry out. Its compact size suits the front of a shaded border or a container planting where a dependable, long-blooming pink astilbe is needed.

common_name: Pink Jewel Astilbe (Compact Arching Light Red-Purple Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade.

directions: Pink Jewel forms an upright, mounded, compact clump of glossy, finely cut foliage topped by gracefully arching inflorescences of light red-purple flowers that open freely and uniformly. Patented by Green Works International B.V. of the Netherlands (US Plant Patent PP16,346) from a chance seedling of two unnamed Astilbe simplicifolia plants, it was chosen for its rapid growth and compact, well-proportioned habit. Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; like other simplicifolia-type astilbes it tolerates somewhat drier conditions than the larger arendsii hybrids but still performs best without letting the soil dry out. Its arching flower form distinguishes it from the stiffer, more upright plumes of many other astilbe cultivars.

common_name: Pretty in Pink Astilbe (Long-Blooming Dwarf Two-Tone Pink Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade.

directions: Pretty in Pink is a compact, clump-forming astilbe with basal rosettes of sharply toothed, rich green leaves and loose, open, arching plumes of two-tone pale and mid-pink flowers carried on dark stems. It is among the longest-blooming astilbes available, holding color for six weeks or more from midsummer into early fall, well beyond the typical two-to-three-week astilbe bloom window. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; its small stature and extended bloom suit it well to patio containers, border edges, and small-space woodland gardens. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor and flowering.

common_name: Baby Pink Astilbe (Compact Soft Pink Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in fertile, evenly moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade.

directions: Baby Pink carries long, airy plumes of soft pastel-pink flowers above a compact mound of dark green, lacy, deeply cut foliage, blooming in midsummer. It shows good resistance to the leaf spot, powdery mildew, and root rot problems that can trouble some older astilbe hybrids, making it a dependable, lower-maintenance choice for a shaded border. Plant in fertile, evenly moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, and divide clumps every three to four years in early spring once they become congested. Its soft color combines well with white- or blue-flowered shade perennials such as brunnera or hosta foliage.

common_name: Mahogany Snow Hellebore (Gold Collection Aging Rose-to-Mahogany Lenten Rose)

planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants in fall or early spring into rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; avoid disturbing established clumps.

directions: Mahogany Snow opens clean, creamy white, outward-facing flowers with strong pink backsides in January, then slowly ages through rose to deep mahogany-pink tones over an unusually long bloom season into March, with individual flowers lasting for weeks. The compact plant has deep green, leathery evergreen foliage on reddish stems, part of the German Gold Collection breeding program that crosses Helleborus niger, H. lividus, and related species for vigor and extended bloom. Plant in rich, humus-laden, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and avoid disturbing established clumps, since hellebores resent transplanting once settled. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter just before the flower stems emerge to show off the long season of slowly shifting color.

common_name: Tangerine Wave Coral Bells (Fox Series Wavy-Edged Orange Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained soil; color is brightest with some direct sun.

directions: Tangerine Wave is a compact, neat Fox Series heuchera bred by UK specialist nursery Plantagogo, with lobed, ruffled, wavy-edged leaves that open bright tangerine-orange and deepen to mahogany as they mature, the color constantly shifting through the season. In full sun the foliage reaches its brightest orange tones, while in shade or part shade it settles into a softer caramel. Airy stems of small, creamy white flowers rise above the foliage in summer and attract bees and other pollinators. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; this cultivar has received the RHS Award of Garden Merit for reliable garden performance and semi-evergreen winter foliage in milder climates.

common_name: Heart of Darkness Foamy Bells (Maroon-and-Silver-Patterned Heucherella)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Heart of Darkness carries green leaves marked with a large central zone of dark maroon surrounded by silvery gray, a pattern that intensifies in cooler weather until only a narrow green margin remains visible around the edges. The loose mound of textured foliage is topped in late spring by branched, spreading flower stems bearing relatively large, showy pink-tinged white flowers well above the leaves. Introduced by Charles Oliver of The Primrose Path in Pennsylvania, it was selected for its unusual, seasonally shifting foliage coloration. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where the dramatic maroon-and-silver pattern shows best against plainer-leaved companions.

common_name: Filigree Lace Foamflower (Deeply Cut Lacy-Leaved Tiarella)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Filigree Lace is a Primrose Path hybrid of Tiarella cordifolia and Tiarella trifoliata, bred for leaves that are cut almost to the center, giving the foliage a lacy, filigree texture unlike the more solid-leaved cordifolia selections. Each leaf carries a distinctive dark purple marking at its base, and the foliage typically turns reddish bronze through autumn and winter, remaining evergreen in milder climates. Short spikes of white flowers rise just above the foliage in spring on stolons that slowly spread the clump outward, making it useful as a woodland groundcover. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade for the best foliage color and texture.

common_name: Butterfly Wings Foamflower (Deeply Cut Maroon-Centered Tiarella)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade.

directions: Butterfly Wings bears foliage cut so deeply into five separate lobes that the two side lobes lift above the central section, giving each leaf the look of a butterfly poised to take flight; the centers are heavily marked with maroon that deepens seasonally. The clump stays tight and non-running, forming a neat mound topped by light pink flowers held on erect stems well above the foliage in spring. Introduced by The Primrose Path in 2001 (US Plant Patent PP13,629), it has been influential as a parent in the breeding of many later cut-leaved, heavily marked Tiarella cultivars. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade, where the dramatic leaf shape and maroon centers show to best advantage.

common_name: Pink Brushes Foamflower (Deep Pink-Flowered Clumping Tiarella)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, medium-moisture, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Pink Brushes was bred by Charles Oliver of The Primrose Path by crossing Tiarella 'Braveheart' with Tiarella 'Spring Bronze', producing deeply lobed leaves with seasonally variable maroon central markings and new growth flushed with purple in early spring. Dense, brush-like racemes of pink, bell-shaped flowers open from pink buds and fade gradually to white, a richer and longer-lasting pink display than many other foamflowers. The non-running clump forms a tidy mound of foliage with flower stalks rising well above the leaves in late April and May. Plant in average, medium-moisture, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where it combines well with hosta and fern companions.
